analysis.one_liner: Repeals the requirement that federal construction contractors pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would end prevailing-wage requirements for workers on federally funded construction, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally financed construction of public buildings and works to pay workers the wage rate that prevails locally for their trade [S2]. This bill would repeal that requirement entirely and wipe out every reference to it in other laws, effective 30 days after enactment, while leaving existing contracts alone [S3]. Contractors could then pay whatever wages they choose on federal projects, generally meaning lower pay for construction workers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal construction contractors and developers gain the most: they could bid lower on government projects by paying crews less than the local prevailing rate. Their workers would bear the cost through reduced pay on federally funded jobs [S2][S3]. Supporters also argue taxpayers benefit through cheaper federal construction, since prevailing-wage rules generally raise bid prices on government contracts.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that laborers and mechanics on federally financed construction be paid the locally prevailing wage, letting contractors set their own pay rates [S2][S3].
Voids every reference to the Davis-Bacon wage requirement in other laws, not just the core statute, so no prevailing-wage mandate would survive in any federally assisted construction program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, who would lose the prevailing-wage floor and see lower take-home pay on those jobs [S2]. Labor unions that negotiate around prevailing-wage standards would also lose leverage.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the wage floor for construction workers on federally funded public buildings and works, reducing their pay on those jobs [S2].

Supporters' main argument is the cost side: prevailing-wage requirements generally push up the price of federal construction, so taxpayers would likely see lower bids after repeal. That potential savings is the strongest honest case for the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Any savings to taxpayers from cheaper federal construction bids would come directly out of the wages of construction workers on those projects. There is no mechanism in the bill to compensate workers or ensure savings are passed to taxpayers rather than absorbed as contractor margin, so the trade runs mostly from workers to contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Good introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act in the House on March 26, 2021 [S1][S5].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction and received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects keep the prevailing-wage floor, and the contractors who would have benefited from paying lower wages did not get the change.

for.name: Rep. Bob Good
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage requirements.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee with no action after referral.

against.name: Building trades labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed Davis-Bacon repeal, which unions consistently fight because prevailing-wage rules anchor pay standards on federal projects.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it; no Democrat supported the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federally financed projects pay below the local prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs and improving bid competitiveness. The gain comes directly out of construction workers' paychecks.
Prevailing-wage rules set a pay floor that union wage and benefit standards ride on; repeal would erode that anchor on federal work and weaken union bargaining position.
